one_liner: Meta's graph-of-codecs compression framework: format-aware compressors for structured data plus a native LZ that decodes about 2.3x faster than zstd -1.
what_it_does: OpenZL builds a specialized compressor from a description of your data (the SDDL data-description language, custom parsers, or training with `zli train`) and writes a self-describing frame that one universal decompressor can read, whatever graph produced it. It has a C11 core with C++17 bindings, a `zli` CLI, a Python extension, and one-pass C APIs (ZL_CCtx_create / ZL_decompress) that look zstd-like but are deliberately not a drop-in: the header comments out a ZS2_compress() shim 'because it is confusing users who think Zstrong is a drop in replacement for Zstd'. For unstructured bytes the 'serial' profile uses a native LZ codec (the default since v0.2.0), and unrecognized input falls back to generic compression.
how_it_is_fast: Compression is modelled as a directed acyclic graph of small codecs (parse into typed field streams, transpose, delta, tokenize, field LZ, entropy coding), so each stream reaches a coder suited to it; that gives better ratio than one generic LZ pass at similar or higher speed on structured data. A trainer (and, in v0.3.0, a 'Compression Transformer' neural selector) picks the graph per dataset. The native LZ engine got its v0.3.0 decode gain from PivCo Huffman, a Huffman layout that stores a bitmap per internal tree node and rebuilds the data bottom-up with SIMD instead of walking the bitstream symbol by symbol (PR #1035: 2574 vs 1416 MB/s decode against huf0 on AVX-512, for 12% slower encode), plus ARM NEON and SVE2 kernels.
when_to_use: Large volumes of structured or columnar data with a known layout (numeric arrays, records, CSV, Parquet, ML checkpoints) where ratio and speed must both beat zstd and you can afford to write an SDDL description or run training.
Read-heavy pipelines on 64-bit servers that want faster decompression than zstd at a similar ratio: v0.3.0 LZ decodes Silesia at 3062 MB/s vs 1254-1345 MB/s for zstd -1.
Numeric streams (8 to 64-bit integers): the v0.3.0 release reports a 7.76x mean ratio over 17.9 GB of numeric files vs 5.75x for zstd -19 and 5.92x for xz -9 (ratio only, no speed given).
Fleets that need one decoder for many dataset-specific compressors, since every frame is decodable by the same universal decompressor.
when_not_to_use: Generic or small text where ratio matters: the native LZ on Silesia trails default zstd -1 on ratio (2.73 vs 2.89), and issue #207 reports a 264,383-byte Twitter JSON file growing to 305,949 bytes with the example JSON path.

When you need a stable wire format or API off release tags: README says API, format and codec set will change, dev-branch commits carry no guarantees, and v0.3.0 bumped the frame format from 24 to 27 and renamed APIs.
32-bit targets: OpenZL requires a 64-bit platform (CMakeLists; issue #342 asks for 32-bit support and is open).
MSVC-only Windows builds: README says MSVC may fail with C2099 on C11 features and recommends clang-cl or MinGW-w64.
Teams that cannot invest in data descriptions or training: the large wins are on described or trained formats; without that, the gain shrinks to the LZ engine's faster decode.

integration.form: static lib (shared optional via OPENZL_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS), plus zli CLI, C++ bindings and Python extension
integration.dependencies: zstd 1.5.7 (git submodule or fetched tarball with SHA-256 check); optional test, benchmark (Google Benchmark), Parquet and Python components
integration.min_toolchain: C11 and C++17 compiler; CMake 3.20.2+ (or the bundled Makefile); clang-cl or MinGW-w64 on Windows
integration.platforms: 64-bit only (x86-64, aarch64; NEON and SVE2 kernels added in v0.3.0; wasm64 via Emscripten)
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the headers read; state lives in explicit ZL_CCtx / ZL_DCtx contexts, so use one context per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: OpenZL frames are not zstd frames and the API differs (ZL_CCtx / ZL_DCtx with a compressor graph); the zstd-style one-call compress was removed on purpose, though ZL_decompress(dst, cap, src, size) is one call

gotchas: The '144% faster than Zstandard' decode figure compares against zstd -1 with windowLog=16, hashLog=14 (the 64K-window row: ratio 2.74, 1254 MB/s); against default zstd -1 (ratio 2.89, 1345 MB/s) the decode gain is about 2.3x (derived from page data) and OpenZL's ratio is lower.

Check optimization flags: issue #163 found the Makefile compiling at -O1 and decompression about 5x slower than zstd; the README now says BUILD_TYPE=OPT is the default, and `make show-config` prints the flags in use.

Default compression is strict: if the input does not match the expected format (e.g. not a multiple of 4 bytes for a 32-bit graph) compression errors out unless ZL_CParam_permissiveCompression is set to fall back to generic compression.

PivCo Huffman is enabled only for inputs of 16 KiB and larger (PR #1035), so small-buffer decode speed is lower than the headline number; inputs of several GB are split into about 16 MB chunks automatically (v0.2.0).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick OpenZL over zstd when your data has a describable structure (numeric columns, records, Parquet) or decode speed dominates and you control both ends; stay on zstd for byte-stream interoperability, a stable format and the best ratio on generic text, and use LZ4 when compression speed matters more than ratio.
verified_claims_summary: First-party release notes (v0.2.0 and v0.3.0) report Silesia at level 1: OpenZL LZ v0.3.0 ratio 2.73, 467 MB/s compress, 3062 MB/s decompress vs zstd -1 with a 64K window 2.74 / 419 / 1254 and plain zstd -1 2.89 / 424 / 1345; the linked gist names an AMD EPYC Genoa at 3 GHz and an internal clang-LTO buck build, with zli and zstd CLI commands for reproduction, but no zstd version or public compiler flags. Trained-compressor speed claims (e.g. 340 MB/s at ratio 2.06 vs zstd 220 MB/s at 1.31) come from Meta's whitepaper, seen only as a search snippet.
status_note: Very active (v0.3.0 on 2026-09-29, last commit 2026-10-02, used in production at Meta), BSD-licensed; treat it as pre-1.0 and pin release tags because the frame format and API still change.
